graduation_requirements.raw_text:
In accordance with Vermont education law and South Burlington School District Graduation Policy, SBHS students will meet the
requirements for graduation when the student demonstrates evidence of proficiency in academic content-areas and student
learning expectations (SLEs) which outline student’s skills and habits across content areas.

Students will be introduced to graduation proficiencies through courses and experiences during their first two years of high school
and assessed at the graduation level via courses and experiences during their final years of high school in the following areas:
● English
● Health
● Math
● Science
● Social Studies: Including Public Issues and Financial Literacy
● Physical Education
● Technology
● Visual and Performing Arts
● World Language

Student Learning Expectations (SLEs):
○ Clear & Effective Communication
○ Self-direction
○ Creative & Practical Problem Solving
○ Responsible & Involved Citizenship
○ Informed & Integrative Thinking

In order to be assessed at the graduation level South Burlington High School1 students must enroll in and successfully complete the
following program minimums. Department specific distribution recommendations and requirements are explained in each
department’s section of this document.

Department Number of Years

Social Studies 3.5**

courses.description: This heterogeneously-grouped course will provide students the opportunity to practice skills that will lead them to proficiency. Our goal is to continue developing students’ reading, writing, speaking, listening, analysis and critical thinking skills. Students will craft narratives, literary analysis essays, and arguments, and write informally to explore ideas; read classic and contemporary literature to better understand themselves and their places in the world; and read books of their own choice with the goal of fostering a community of readers. Students will be pushed to stretch their learning to the best of their abilities.

American Studies is an interdisciplinary course in which students learn through collaboration, writing, and critical thinking. The timeline of the course begins at Reconstruction and ends with the 21st century. Students will be reading literature of and about the time periods studied and will reflect on how events of the past shape the present day. A variety of teaching techniques and strategies are used throughout the course to help students seek answers to fundamental questions such as: What has it meant to be (an) American throughout this country’s history? How have Americans defined and redefined the concepts of freedom and rights throughout our history? All students will have the opportunity to opt into honors level work and complete that work to earn the honors distinction on their transcript at the end of the course.

courses.description: The United States = the U.S.= Us; however, does “us” mean all of us? When considering the post-Civil War era, westward expansion, our industrialization, the Great Depression, Civil Rights, Black Lives Matter, are the same lines of justice and law drawn consistently for everyone? What makes a good story? Does the American classic To Kill a Mockingbird tell the story of race in America as honestly and importantly as Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun? Honors American Studies is a combination of 10th grade Honors U.S. History and Honors English 10, 2 credits in one course. We meet daily. We learn much through cooperation and small-group work. We study exciting books. Whether discussing a document from 200 years ago, or debating the recent storming of the Capitol, we exhibit strong feelings and beliefs, making us better citizens. Self-discipline and reliability in completing homework are recommended skills for the course.

courses.description: How have writers of the past and present used nonfiction, fiction, poetry, and drama to communicate ideas? How can we employ the methods of these writers in our own communication? How can the process of writing lead to insight and meaning? Students start their work reading books during the summer and finish with an opportunity to earn college credit by taking a national three-hour examination given by the College Board. This course focuses on the development and revision of evidence-based analytic and argumentative writing and the analysis of nonfiction texts. Through discussion, writing, and presentations, we will build on the knowledge students bring to the course as well as prepare them for future courses in college. Self-discipline and reliability in completing homework are recommended skills for the course. (It is very strongly recommended that students enrolled in Advanced Placement courses take the Advanced Placement exam.)

How does understanding what we read help us understand ourselves, others, and life? Advanced Placement English Literature requires students to go beyond comprehension to an understanding of how writing achieves its effects. Students start their work reading at least two books during the summer and finish with an opportunity to earn college credit by taking a national three-hour examination given by the College Board. The course presumes students’ willingness to work to understand sophisticated prose and poetry from the late 16th century to the present. Students should also look forward to the challenge of sustained analysis of texts and frequent participation in full-class discussion. Students write some long essays on literary topics, and they write many timed essays to prepare themselves for the AP examination, always remembering writing means what it says. It is recommended that students enrolling in AP Literature possess strong writing skills and a willingness to become a better reader. (It is very strongly recommended that students enrolled in Advanced Placement courses take the Advanced Placement exam.)

This course will focus on all four proficiency areas. Students can expect an engaging opening to class each day with a poem read by the teacher and a creative quick write. The purpose of this course will be to dive into and enjoy full-length works of literature, both fiction and nonfiction. Genres will include Realistic Fiction, Thriller, Contemporary Young Adult, Science Fiction and more. Nonfiction types will include Nonfiction Narrative, Autobiographical Essays and Memoirs. There will also be an opportunity for students to engage in a choice genre-exploration. Students will write both creative fiction and argument essays. Students will be expected to engage in full class discussions on the current book and participate in listening and speaking activities. Vocabulary will be introduced throughout each unit and words will be tied to our current literature.

How do we effectively communicate our ideas through storytelling? In this course, students will explore writing short stories, poetry, scripts, flash memoirs, and graphic novels. Writers will work on the communication of ideas, stylistic techniques, experimentation with language, editing, and proofreading. We’ll study and analyze writing techniques of authors and then apply these techniques. We will employ a workshop model of sharing our writing with each other in a supportive, collaborative environment as we work together to develop speaking and listening skills and refine writing craft and personal voice as writers. Assessment is based on effort, improvement, participation, and willingness to give and receive feedback. Come to this course ready to write! Writing, language, and speaking and listening PBGRs are addressed.

courses.description: Why is it important to speak well in public? What characterizes constructive criticism? This course prepares you for real life speaking opportunities in your future. How do we know when we are effective listeners? How can we improve our speaking skills? Students who take this course determine their own goals and use teacher feedback and peer feedback to help reach those goals. This course includes instruction and assessment for Extemporaneous Speaking, Manuscript Speaking, and Impromptu Speaking. Additionally, students will create a slideshow and showcase their speaking skills as they present with their visuals. Everybody is successful in becoming a better speaker.
courses.notes: Semester elective

courses.description: The class is designed to show students how film is a form of literature. By viewing classic and modern films, students will learn that film and written literature have many elements in common, but that film has additional visual and aural elements that contribute meaning. Students will develop an appreciation for the interaction of film elements such as scripting, directing, acting, producing, lighting, sound, music, editing, cinematography, special effects, set design, and costuming. Students will learn film-analysis techniques such as mise en scene and point of view. Over the course of this class, students will engage with films on multiple levels, culminating with the creation of a film project of their own.
courses.notes: Semester elective

courses.description: This course examines the complex and indefinable nature of human behavior as well as the social, political and economic factors that helped Hitler, and other oppressors in history, rise to power. We stretch our thinking by considering why genocides continue to occur and if we are obligated to work to stop oppression. Holocaust Studies explores human behavior from historical and literary perspectives. Students will work to grow as contributing participants in class and develop as moral philosophers, critical consumers of information, and civic agents. This course asks you to read, write, and participate as part of a learning community. Students will have the opportunity to challenge themselves, and if they meet the outlined requirement, earn honors level on their transcript.

courses.description: The College Bound program is designed for first-generation college bound students to decrease barriers in access to college. A first-generation student is defined as being from a family in which neither parent has graduated from a four-year college or university. The purpose of the program is to provide support to these sophomores and juniors in developing and attaining their future goals. What are the steps involved in researching and selecting colleges? How does a student pay for college? What other options are available after high school? The group focuses on exploration during the sophomore year, touring colleges across Vermont. Junior year is more specific education and information about the application and financial aid processes. Students who identify themselves as first generation students are invited to join at the beginning of their sophomore year.

courses.description: The Special Education program aims to develop the skills and independence of students with disabilities who are in need of specialized instruction. In order to receive special services a student must meet Vermont State eligibility requirements for special education. Each student’s program is based on an Individualized Education Plan (IEP), which is developed with a team that includes parents, the student, teachers, and a special educator. Special educators and other trained staff provide instruction in basic skill areas, and students work toward mastering the goals outlined in their IEPs. Specialized instruction is often provided in regular classes through the co-teaching model, where general and special educators teach the skills and content together. The special education program also offers transition planning and community-based experiences for older students who require support to prepare for post-secondary education, employment, and independent living.

courses.description: Enhanced Study is a small class taught by trained special educators where eligible students receive direct instruction in the area of structured literacy and functional skills. These courses provide individualized instruction in the areas of basic reading, fluency, and comprehension, as well as executive functioning skills. Students continue to develop their literacy and executive functioning skills that will enable them to better access course content across disciplines.

courses.description: The Progressive Program is an alternative program for 9th and 10th grade students, located within the high school. The program provides academic and behavioral support to students who are likely to benefit from a more structured program with fewer transitions throughout the school day. Students may be part of the core group or participate in different aspects of the program. Academic instruction is provided in an alternative format by general education teachers in English, Social Studies, Science, Math and Physical Education. Study and social skills are an integral part of the program, and there is a general focus on self-exploration and team building in order to provide students with the skills they need to succeed in the general education environment. Ongoing parental involvement is an important part of this program, and there is a referral process for students to participate that is typically initiated by special education case managers or guidance counselors in 8th or 9th grade for the following year.

courses.description: The Leap program offers specific courses in an alternative format to the larger mainstream environment for 11th and 12th grade students, with smaller classes and more intensive support. The program is flexible and students can take a mix of regular or alternative classes. Leap offers alternative courses in English, Public Issues and World stAffairs, and Financial Literacy. Students can work at their own pace and additional support and structure that some students need in order to meet graduation requirements and build transition skills for their post-graduation pursuits.

courses.department: Alternative Programs and Student Support Programs
courses.description: The SBHS Transition Academy (TA) is a flexible program that meets the needs of our students with more intensive special needs. Transition Academy is less of a set program or sequence of courses, and more of an evolving system of support that prepares students with identified needs for life after high school. In later years, the Transition Academy provides a wide range of opportunities and support, including community-based programming, independent living skills, employment skills, and joining with other schools to participate in specialized programs that create a community for students with similar needs. These experiences meet the needs of older students who may require programming beyond the traditional high school experience to prepare for their future education, employment, and independent living.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: The Wolf Tracks Program supports complex students from 6th through 12th grade and creates a safe, inclusive, and supportive learning environment that meets the unique needs of every student. Many of our students require a space where they feel a sense of belonging before they can fully engage in learning. By fostering a culture of understanding and respect, we empower students to regulate, build independence, and develop a lifelong love of learning. Wolf Tracks is less of a set program or sequence of courses, and more of an evolving system of support that prepares students with identified needs.

courses.description: An increase in RISK creates a decrease in SAFETY. How, then, does a driver reduce risk? A responsible driver is a defensive driver, and the best driver is a proactive (and not reactive) driver. In the state of Vermont, Driver Education is mandatory for a junior operator’s license. Driver Education is offered at South Burlington High School during the academic year as a .25 credit course, and the following qualifications and stipulations apply: 1. In situations involving over enrollment, priority for the opportunity will be given in descending order with senior students having first priority, juniors second, and so on. Within a class, priority will be given on an age basis with the older students receiving first priority. 2. It will be necessary to schedule student’s driving time during their unscheduled periods of the school day. 3. Because the specified amount of time for course qualification is six DRIVER EDUCATION PROGRAM actual hours of “behind-the-wheel” experience, students should expect to give out-of-school time to this need if necessary. 4. Since the state of Vermont mandates thirty hours of classroom instruction, students cannot miss more than four classroom instruction periods for non-school related reasons. 5. Students must obtain permits prior to the first class. Placement in Driver Education courses cannot be guaranteed by the time students are eligible for a license. If you wish to be considered for participation in the Driver Education Program and you meet the qualifications which apply, sign up for this course on your registration form as you would for any other course.
courses.notes: HOMEWORK EXPECTATIONS FOR DRIVER EDUCATION It is strongly recommended that each student receive an additional 50 hours of supervised (parental) behind-the-wheel practice to supplement the six hours received during school.

Through the lens of Early American History, students will explore the ideas of identity, culture, and pivotal events to gain a deeper understanding of the complexity of today’s current issues. Students will analyze how the past influences our current reality and will think about how they can make change to create a more inclusive society. Benchmark units include National History Day and the Bernie Sanders Essay Contest.

How do literary works reflect history? Do the times create the people or do the people create the times? Honors American Studies is an intensive, interdisciplinary pre-AP course in which students learn through group cooperation, writing, and critical thinking. This course endeavors to reinforce the role literature plays in telling the story of American history. Students should expect a rigorous content level and pace. This course demands greater independence and responsibility, focusing on deeper learning and the development of higher level thinking skills. This course uses an AP level textbook.

courses.description: In American History Through Film students will explore the relationship between United States cultural and social history through the medium of film. Through watching, discussing, and analyzing films students will learn how films have both reflected American culture and influenced cultural change. Additionally, a portion of the class will be devoted to the history of film in the United States. Students will encounter the development of film technology, popular films within the context of the times, and examine broader themes and genres with the goal of becoming critical consumers of film and visual media.

courses.description: Economics is a semester-long course covering topics such as economic systems, monetary policy and the role of government in our economy, how markets work, investing and the stock market, the global economy, and current economic events. During this semester, students will examine questions such as: How are economic decisions made? How does the relationship between supply and demand affect prices? What is money? What is globalization? Is college worth it? What criteria do you consider when making personal economic choices?

This course attempts to explore the definition of a democracy and how the organization of our government promotes those democratic ideals. Students will investigate the impact of political parties, the media, and the major institutions of our government – the Presidency, the Congress, and the Supreme Court. Two of the most relevant questions addressed are: How can a citizen be an effective participant in the democratic system? What is the proper balance between the preservation of civil liberties and the need for order and security? (It is very strongly recommended that students enrolled in Advanced Placement courses take the Advanced Placement exam.)

AP Psychology is a year-long course that investigates the scientific study of the behavior and mental processes of human beings and other animals. Students will learn about core psychological principles, influential theorists, and each of the major subfields within psychology. Additionally, students will discover the ethics and methods that psychologists use in their science and practice. Within each unit of study, students will address essential questions that will guide their understanding; for example: How do groups impact individuals? How does stress influence health and behavior? What motivates human behavior? (It is very strongly recommended that students enrolled in Advanced Placement courses take the Advanced Placement exam.)

Students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes from 1200 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical connections; and utilizing reasoning about comparison, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course provides six themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: humans and the environment, cultural developments and interactions, governance, economic systems, social interactions and organization, and technology and innovation. PIWA is a required one-semester course that covers local and world affairs by examining how societies define themselves, what action democratic societies take to accommodate differing perspectives of their citizens, and how the past influences future affairs. Each student will spend the semester completing Project Citizen, which will help students address the questions: How do I use my voice as a citizen? What are the rights and responsibilities of an American citizen? Students will take practical action working to implement and change public policy based on their own research.

courses.description: What is the essential role of play for human beings? How did sports evolve over time? What role have sports played in addressing issues of global concern? Are sports an avenue for equality? Through this course students will learn the historical importance of games and sports in human society. Much of the course will focus on the role of sports in America and how sports and athletes have helped to address issues of inequality both at home and abroad.

What is unique about business ventures in the 21st century? Have you ever wondered about what makes a business successful and sustainable? What can we learn from ‘Shark Tank’ and ‘The Apprentice’? This introductory class helps students learn basic business concepts and then apply these skills in hands-on projects that solve real-world situations. Students will also practice these techniques with case studies, computer simulations, field trips and other interactive methods. This is an excellent class for any student who may be interested in a future in business or who wants to be more successful in DECA while earning a technology credit. Every student should take this class! Students will navigate through real-life financial situations using case studies, computer simulations, and other interactive methods. Topics include banking, investments, credit cards, car loans, housing, taxes, insurance, budgeting and having enough left at the end of the month to save for a vacation! Don’t be caught not knowing how to make ends meet once you leave high school! Instead, get a jump start on making and keeping your first million.

courses.description: Math 1 is designed to engage all students with opportunities to explore data, patterns, shape, and change in realistic contexts and situations. Students will develop an understanding of algebraic, geometric and statistical reasoning through a problem solving approach. Each unit focuses on the overarching theme that patterns are the foundation of mathematics and that these patterns can be communicated through multiple representations. Math 1 is designed to capitalize on students’ strengths and intuition to build capacity for deeper mathematical understanding. This course, taught over two years instead of one, is designed for students who need extra support in their first year or two of high school to better ensure success in mathematics. Students who complete this course will be prepared to take Math 2. Membership in this course must be approved by a committee of the SBHS Mathematics CAS, Student Support Services CAS, and SBSD Math Coordinator.

courses.description: This course begins with a unit on conditional probability. Following the unit on probability, students begin their work with quadratic functions and equations. The second and third units expand what students learned in the previous course about functions and solving equations to include quadratics. The course then transitions to two geometry units centered around similarity and right triangle trigonometry. This leads to an introduction to trigonometry using right triangles, which will be expanded to trigonometric functions in the next course. Next, students derive volume formulas and study the effect of dilation on both area and volume. They connect ideas from algebra and geometry through coordinate geometry, using the structure of the coordinate plane to review theorems and skills from prior units.

courses.description: In this concept-focused course, students explore polynomial and rational functions, progress to exponential functions and logarithms, and delve into graphically and algebraically transforming functions—all with a focus on real-world problem-solving. Students will investigate topics in trigonometry including circular relationships, radian measures, and periodic functions, applying these concepts to practical scenarios. The final unit emphasizes statistical inference, mastering the analysis of real-world data with normal distributions and developing critical thinking skills.

courses.description: As the title suggests, this course is meant to prepare students for calculus in their next year of high school. In this concept-focused course, students explore polynomial and rational functions, progress to exponential functions and logarithms, and delve into graphically and algebraically transforming functions—all with a focus on real-world problem-solving. Students will investigate topics in trigonometry including circular relationships, radian measures, inverse functions, and reciprocal functions, applying these concepts to practical scenarios. Students further explore trigonometry through the solving of trigonometric equations and proving trigonometric identities. Because of the additional topics covered, this course will move at a faster pace than Math 3.

courses.description: This course provides seniors an opportunity to improve their skills and alleviate the need for remediation in college. The Vermont State Colleges System (VSCS) has agreed that successful completion of this course will qualify students to enroll in credit-bearing college math at any VSCS school without the need for remediation or an Accuplacer test score. This course will help Vermont high school students achieve college and career readiness before leaving high school. In addition, EMC2 will provide an opportunity for students to achieve graduation proficiency in critical math content and practices. Using principles from the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM), and supported by the Math Association of America (MAA), this course is designed to be project/task based with guided student discussion and ‘debate’. Concepts are not taught by giving students algorithms but rather by discovering those algorithms within the tasks presented. The curriculum is also designed to have a ‘gradual release’ process whereby teachers guide the process early, set up classroom climate and expectations, and gradually the units are more and more student led. This model strengthens student skills for post-secondary endeavors. Students will be asked to assess their own understanding, learn where and how to seek support when necessary, and gradually become more independent learners.

courses.description: In the fashion industry, who decides what’s “in” and what’s “out?” Fashion design is a competitive and creative market that historically has been driven by popular culture. This course introduces students to fashion design, allowing students to become designers themselves. Students will explore the history of fashion design, create fashion drawings, learn sewing and approaches to apparel construction to bring “runway” fashion concepts to final form.
courses.credits_text: .5 credit in technology or .5 credit in art
courses.fulfills_text: .5 credit in technology or .5 credit in art

courses.description: Create with clay! This one semester course is designed for students interested in a three-dimensional approach to making art. Traditional clay hand-building techniques such as slab, pinch, coil and sculpture will be covered. Students will also learn basic pottery terminology and glaze applications. The elements of art will be used to guide the assignments and to ensure that the work has a strong visual appeal.
courses.notes: Visual Art; Intro level

courses.description: Express yourself! This is a one-semester course offered to students who have an interest in exploring paint as a specific medium. Students will work from life and visual resources. They will refer to artists from the 20th century, working in realistic, abstract, and nonrepresentational styles, to create their own expressive paintings. Recommended Prep: Art I or Draw It.
courses.notes: Visual Art; Intermediate level; prerequisite stated as Recommended Prep

courses.description: Engage and apply your creativity! Be expressive and practice your artistic skills! Art II is designed for students who wish to pursue art for personal interest, in college, or as a career. It provides preparation for further study in the visual arts (design, architecture, computer graphics, etc.). Students will develop advanced skills and create works of art to build their portfolios. Sketchbook assignments help students continue to apply concepts and develop individual style. Required Prep: Art I, Draw It, or by teacher recommendation.
courses.prerequisites: Art I, Draw It, or by teacher recommendation
courses.notes: Visual Art; Intermediate level; prerequisite stated as Required Prep

courses.description: Discover and develop your own style! Learn to integrate the traditional techniques of pottery with your own personal development as a clay artist. Pottery II is designed for students interested in further exploration of clay as a three-dimensional medium. Some sculpture, hand building, and wheel work will be covered in individual and group projects. Students will also explore glaze options and consider cultural inspiration. Required Prep: Pottery I
courses.notes: Visual Art; Intermediate level; prerequisite stated as Required Prep

courses.description: Apply skills and techniques and uncover your own artistic voice. These courses are designed for those students who wish to pursue art in college, as a career, or for personal interest. They provide excellent preparation for further study in visual arts, design, architecture, or digital arts etc.. Students often have more freedom and choice of subject matter, media, and approach within the structure of assignments. This class helps students prepare portfolios for art school admission. Art III is open to juniors and seniors who have completed Art II. Art IV is designed for students who have completed Art III. Required Prep: Art II for course 720, Art III for course 725.

courses.description: Comics and Graphic Novels are unique because they communicate primarily through drawn images. Using web-based applications and industry-standard software, this course provides students with the skills to create comics that express their individuality. Projects require storytelling, creative expression, experimentation, editing, and the study of comic themes and comic art. Each class will produce a collaborative anthology that will be printed, published, and promoted. Check out the 2020 Graphic Novels Anthology This class satisfies the Information Technology 0.5 credit required for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: This class satisfies the Information Technology 0.5 credit required for graduation.

courses.description: Is a picture really worth a thousand words? What does a “good” photograph look like? Students in Photography will spend the semester exploring these questions by taking their own photographs and viewing/discussing those created by their classmates and other photographers. This course uses photography as a means to investigate the students’ world by exploring the design process, from idea through execution to critical evaluation. This class satisfies the Information Technology 0.5 credit required for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: This class satisfies the Information Technology 0.5 credit required for graduation.
courses.notes: Media Arts

courses.description: LIghts! Camera! Action! Today, anyone may feel that they can become a filmmaker by using a camcorder or phone. In this course, students gain new perspectives on what really makes a filmmaker. Using storyboarding and shot lists, learning the basics of camera work, and applying editing techniques, students will compose and finalize their own videos. Students will work in a variety of video genres, using industry-standard editing programs in conjunction with each project, allowing students complete creative ownership over the video-making process. This class satisfies the Information Technology 0.5 credit required for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: This class satisfies the Information Technology 0.5 credit required for graduation.

courses.description: Ever feel your pulse quicken while looking at a snowboard catalog? Well, it isn’t just because of the pretty people. By understanding the demographics of their intended audience, savvy designers manipulate the principles and elements of design to create graphics to market all types of products and information. Effective graphic design can stir emotions, provide detail, communicate a brand and, yes, even excite us. Now you, too, can learn design strategies, using industry standard software to develop graphics that can grab a viewer’s attention. This class satisfies the Information Technology 0.5 credit required for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: This class satisfies the Information Technology 0.5 credit required for graduation.

courses.description: This is a large instrumental ensemble open to all 9th and 10th grade woodwind, brass, and percussion players without an audition. The Concert Band rehearses and performs music of all styles and performs three to four concerts each year. You are welcome to join if you have some experience playing a band instrument or if you have taken lessons on another instrument (piano or a string instrument). Students enrolled in this ensemble have the opportunity to travel with the band (London and Scotland in April 2025!) and to participate in the District Instrumental Festival.
courses.notes: Music Courses; Open to all 9th and 10th grade woodwind, brass, and percussion players without an audition; offered at the same time as Mixed Chorus so students may take both for .5 credit each

courses.description: This is a small, full-year choral ensemble open to all 9th graders and first-year choral students. No previous experience is required. This course will focus on learning and performing standard choral repertoire, refining basic musicianship, theory skills, and individual vocal and choral technique. This ensemble will prepare its own music as well as the Concert Chorus music for performance at least three times per school year. Grades will be assigned on an individual basis, based on classroom work, work outside of class, and skill assessment. Students enrolled in this ensemble also have the opportunity to participate in All-State, New England, and District Choral Festivals.
courses.notes: Music Courses; Offered at the same time as Concert Band so students may take both for .5 credit each

courses.description: This is a large instrumental ensemble open to woodwind, brass, and percussion players in grades 9-12, by audition only. Students in this ensemble will learn challenging wind ensemble literature and work on refining individual as well as ensemble musical skills. The Symphonic Band performs three to four concerts each year, and includes participation in a music competition. Students are expected to practice their music assigned for performance as well as classroom assignments.
courses.notes: Music Courses; By audition only; offered at the same time as Concert Chorus so students may take both for .5 credit each

courses.description: Concert Chorus is a large, four-part vocal ensemble focused on the study and performance of standard choral literature. Students enrolled in this class will also continue refining basic musicianship and theory skills and their individual vocal and choral technique. There are usually three concert performances per school year in addition to participation options in All-State, New England, and District Choral Festivals. Students are expected to practice the music assigned for performance as well as complete any written assignments. This is a full-year, performance-based offering. Students are assessed on an individual and sometimes ensemble basis. It is open to students in grades 10-12, who have had prior choral experience. If you are new to the district or to the choral program, you must interview with the director. Grade 9 students are welcome to audition following completion of one year in mixed chorus.
courses.notes: Music Courses; Offered at the same time as Symphonic Band so students may take both for .5 credit each

courses.description: This is a small choral ensemble focused on the study of more challenging repertoire, ranging from Renaissance to Jazz, different styles, different genres, and different cultures. Students may enroll in this course upon successful completion of either MIXED CHORUS or CONCERT CHORUS with the RECOMMENDATION of the instructor only. This happens at the end of the previous school year. It is a year-long commitment. These singers have performed for WCAX Channel 3, Dessert Night, graduation, faculty meetings, and dedications. In addition, this ensemble participates in VT American Choral Directors Association Mid-Winter Madrigal Festival, Vermont All State Music Festival, New England Music Festival, and they travel extensively. It is recommended that students be enrolled in Concert Chorus and have a basic knowledge of music theory and choral technique. Students will be assessed on an individual basis as well as ensemble skills.
courses.notes: Music Courses

courses.description: This is a small, select wind ensemble open to anyone in grades 9-12 by audition only. This “catch-all” class is focused on intense musical study in every aspect, including theory, ear training, challenging wind ensemble and chamber music repertoire. This class is recommended for the serious instrumental student who would like a challenge.
courses.notes: Music Courses; By audition only

courses.description: You don’t need to already play the piano or read music to take this class. If you don’t play the piano but always wanted to learn, this is your chance! If you already play and want to learn more about music theory and harmony, this is for you. This class will be divided into two groups: those who cannot read music and those who can. You’ll feel comfortable practicing on a digital piano with headsets without others hearing you. Curriculum will include learning to read music and understand music theory while playing simple pop songs of your choice with two hands. Every Friday is “Fun Friday” where you’ll experience interesting and amazing things happening in the music world.
courses.notes: Music Courses

courses.description: This is an immersive Theater Production and Acting class, where creativity meets craftsmanship on and off the stage. Through a blend of hands-on experience and theoretical exploration, students will discover the artistry behind both production and acting. In the production segment, students will learn the intricacies of set design, lighting, sound, marketing and stage management as they support the SBHS Fall Musical. The acting component will focus on honing performance skills, exploring diverse acting methods, and cultivating a deep understanding of character interpretation. Through improvisation, scene work, and monologue performances, students will refine their ability to embody roles and connect authentically with their characters. No prerequisite is required. Students will be asked to participate in the production during after school hours.
courses.notes: Music Courses list (Theater/Drama)

courses.description: “Improv” or Improvisation is a form of performance either on stage or in speech that uses idea generation to create work in the moment. Performances are not written. The core principles of acceptance are practiced to extemporaneously build content through collaboration. This class introduces the concept of “Yes, And” in improvisation. Using group exercises and games, students will explore impulse & spontaneity. They will be reacting, listening, taking risks, finding agreement (making & accepting offers) and being present in the moment. They will learn the basic building blocks of improvisation in a supportive environment that embraces the idea of trusting yourself and failing joyfully. Techniques learned in this class are easily transferable and will improve communication skills, conversation strategies and foster professional development. This is a one-semester course. No prerequisite is required. Students may repeat the course, but only with the instructor’s approval.

courses.description: Students learn why it is important to understand another culture and how one can use Spanish to enrich one’s life outside the classroom. This course is an introduction to the language and culture of the Spanish- speaking world. A high level of student participation is expected through the use of materials and activities designed to enable the student to use the language for communication. Special emphasis is placed on the national standards for communication, cultures, connections, comparisons, and communities.

Students learn: 1) how cultural legacies shape behavior and world views in the multiple countries and regions where Spanish is spoken; 2) how knowing a world language enhances career opportunities; 3) how learning another language increases understanding of one’s native language. This course is a continuation of previous courses. Emphasis is placed on helping the student to communicate orally according to the basic national standards. Continued guided practice on grammatical structures and vocabulary expansion is used to increase novice-level proficiency in all skill areas.

Students learn: 1) that the world is moving toward a global community; 2) it is increasingly important to attain proficiency in another world language; 3) to engage in conversations, interpret authentic materials, and present concepts in another language. This course is a continuation of Spanish, presenting the more complex structures of intermediate Spanish, increasing the student’s communicative vocabulary, and expanding the broad cultural themes of Spanish. Students use all simple tenses. This class is taught primarily in Spanish.

Students learn that the study of a world language not only serves as a vehicle to explore foreign cultures and ways of thinking, but also as a frame of reference for better understanding English-speaking cultures by comparison. This is a continuation of the Spanish 3 program. The emphasis is placed on the study of more advanced grammatical topics. Acquisition of active and passive vocabulary through selected readings is also a major objective of this course. Written compositions based on the reading selections are required. Students work throughout the year with materials which are specifically designed to correlate with the ACTFL oral proficiency guidelines and the national standards. Students are expected to communicate successfully in basic survival situations. The class is conducted in Spanish.

Students learn: 1) that the study of foreign cultures helps us better understand our own by comparison; 2) that cultural objectivity promotes tolerance and compassion; 3) what determines cultural identity. This course is equivalent to a second-year college course and is taught almost exclusively in Spanish. It is intended for those students who have chosen to continue to develop their language proficiency in the four skill areas of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students are prepared to critically analyze the form and content of authentic works, have discussions on current topics, write essays in different formats, and hold daily conversations, all in Spanish.

Spanish 6 focuses on developing high-level communication skills in Spanish in an immersion environment. Students in Spanish 6 can expect to increase their vocabulary, as well as their oral and written proficiency levels through small-group work and conversation, while speaking and hearing Spanish 100% of the time..

This course is an introduction to the studies of the French language and the French-speaking world. A high level of student participation is expected through the use of materials and activities designed to enable the student to use the language for communication. ACTFL standards for communication, cultures, and comparisons guide curricular topics of study. The goal is to become proficient at the novice-mid level according to the ACTFL proficiency scale.

This course is a continuation of studies of the French language and the French-speaking world. A high level of student participation is expected through the use of materials and activities designed to enable the student to use the language for communication. ACTFL standards for communication, cultures, and comparisons guide curricular topics of study. The goal is to become proficient at the novice-high level according to the ACTFL proficiency scale.

This course is a continuation of studies of the French language and the French-speaking world. A high level of student participation is expected through the use of materials and activities designed to enable the student to use the language for communication. ACTFL standards for communication, cultures, and comparisons guide curricular topics of study. The goal is to become proficient at the intermediate-low level according to the ACTFL proficiency scale.

This course is a continuation of studies of the French language and the French-speaking world. A high level of student participation is expected through the use of materials and activities, which are designed to enable the student to use the language for communication. Special emphasis is placed on the ACTFL standards for communication, cultures, and comparisons. The goal is to become proficient at the intermediate-mid level and beyond according to the ACTFL proficiency scale. This course is conducted entirely in French.

This course is a continuation of studies of the French language and the French-speaking world. A high level of student participation is expected through the use of materials and activities, which are designed to enable the student to use the language for communication. Special emphasis is placed on the ACTFL standards for communication, cultures, and comparisons. In this class, students continue to build skills at the intermediate-mid level, and beyond, according to the ACTFL proficiency scale. This course is conducted entirely in French.

This course is a continuation of studies of the French language and the French-speaking world. A high level of student participation is expected through the use of materials and activities, which are designed to enable the student to use the language for communication. Special emphasis is placed on the ACTFL standards for communication, cultures, and comparisons. The goal is to become proficient at the intermediate-high level according to the ACTFL proficiency scale. This course is conducted entirely in French.

Students learn that it is important to participate in a global community where basic needs are expressed and met and information is exchanged. The primary purpose of this course is to establish the importance of participating in a global community. Effective communication skills help students express their basic needs and have these needs met. Students learn basic tenses while focusing on vocabulary acquisition. Reinforcement of classwork is done through the exploration of a variety of cultural topics.

Students learn about other traditions and customs to increase their awareness of cultural perspectives. They learn how cultural legacies shape behavior and world views in the multiple countries and regions where German is spoken. Special emphasis is placed on the national standards for communication, cultures, connections, comparisons, and communities. Most classwork is conducted entirely in German with emphasis on increasing conversational skills. The cultural focus builds on German 1 with greater focus on everyday life: shopping, describing one’s community, ,, buying a train ticket, understanding current events, and talking about past events.

Students learn: 1) that the world is moving toward a global community; 2) it is increasingly important to attain proficiency in another world language; 3) to engage in conversations, interpret authentic materials, and present concepts in another language. The course is taught primarily in German. Upon completion of German 3, students will have learned all the basic German grammar. Emphasis is still primarily on the oral mastery of material, but students write short compositions and Nacherzaehlungen regularly. Topics include travel, living in a German- speaking country, and how Germans celebrate holidays.

Students learn that the study of a world language not only serves as a vehicle to explore foreign cultures and ways of thinking, but as a frame of reference for better understanding English and American “cultures” by comparison. Students are given a thorough review of German grammar. Students work throughout the year with materials which are specifically designed to correlate with the ACTFL oral proficiency guidelines and the national standards. Students are expected to communicate successfully in basic survival situations. Longer works of German literature are read and discussed including folk tales, plays, short stories,, and articles on contemporary problems in the German speaking countries. Compositions are regularly written in response to films that address the complexities of Germany’s past, and how the past informs the present. German 4 is taught almost exclusively in German.

Latin 1 provides the necessary background in the language to enable the student to read simple Latin. An attempt to understand how language (any language) operates is revealed through a comparison of a highly inflected language like Latin with a much less inflected language, English. In building vocabulary, the importance of English derivatives is constantly stressed. Basic grammar of declensions of nouns and conjugations of verbs plus other points of syntax are covered. The readings cover a broad overview of ancient Roman daily life and culture and form a basis for discussion of its influence on American and English culture. Additional cultural material includes the mythology of Ovid, Livy, and Vergil. Included are hands-on projects to learn about the culture of the ancient Roman world as well as to give students opportunities to acquire skills for real-world experiences. All work aligns with the Standards for Classical Language Learning.

Latin 2 builds on the student’s knowledge from Latin 1 in an effort to read adapted Latin and gain perspective on Modern culture. This will be done through adapted source readings and modern readings based on daily life and popular mythology of the Romans; in particular, the entertainment and the great heroic myths. Grammar will focus on declining nouns and adjectives from all declensions and the conjugation of verbs in the present, perfect and future tenses; the passive and active voices; and the use of participles. Culture and history will be taught through readings which focus on the deeds of the Great Romans involved in the Punic Wars, the Rise and Fall of Caesar, and the creation of the Roman Empire. English vocabulary will be built through close attention to etymology and the use of prefixes and suffixes from Latin. Latin 2 addresses many of the common core principles in English Language Arts as well as various math and science standards.

Latin 3 will focus on building the student’s ability to read adapted reading from native sources. Building on the topics covered in Latin 2, students will progress from the Ecce Romani text to using a variety of open-source readings on the myths and Deities of the Roman people. Grammar content will include advanced and more specific uses of all cases, the use of pronouns, and irregular adjectives in all declensions. Heavy emphasis will be placed on learning the hortatory and jussive subjunctive moods, as well as indirect commands, purpose and result clauses. Culture will cover the geography of the eastern Empire, and the heroes of the Republic, and Early Empire through level appropriate, adapted readings. Students will continue to investigate the English derivatives from Latin roots, suffixes, and prefixes, as well as a small selection of Greek derivatives also via roots, suffixes, and prefixes.

Latin 4 will continue to build the student’s ability to read adapted selections from native sources, with a transition to reading original texts. Grammar content will focus on ACTFL classical language standards to include advanced uses of the ablative and dative cases, introduction of the passive mood, and review of the hortatory and jussive subjunctive moods. New material will include the uses of the subjunctive in the present and imperfect tenses. We will work towards the goal of translating authentic Latin in poetry, drama and prose. Culture will cover the geography of the Northern Empire with a focus on reading Caesar’s De Bello Gallico and selections of Livy’s History of Rome.

Students learn that it is important to participate in a global community where basic needs are expressed and met and information is exchanged. The primary purpose of this course is to establish the importance of participating in a global community. Effective communication skills help students express their basic needs, and have these needs met. This class is designed to get students speaking Japanese. Students can expect to be able to negotiate greetings; to describe family, hobbies, and daily routines. Students talk about food, prices, and schedules and learn two of three writing systems used in Japan (Hiragana and Katakana with 46 symbols each). There will be much emphasis on cultural context to support communication and interaction with native speakers.

Students learn about other traditions and customs to increase their awareness of cultural perspectives. They learn how cultural legacies shape behavior and world views in the multiple countries and regions where Japanese is spoken. Special emphasis is placed on the national standards for communication, cultures, connections, comparisons, and communities. This course expands the student’s communication skills in spoken Japanese and builds a basic (50-80) repertoire of Kanji. Topics from Japanese 1 are reviewed with more in-depth vocabulary and structures. New topics in language and culture include regional divisions and specialties within Japan, school subjects and grades, folktales, and language necessary for participating in travel and entertainment in Japan.

Students learn: 1) that the world is moving toward a global community; 2) it is increasingly important to attain proficiency in another world language; 3) to engage in conversations, interpret authentic materials, and present concepts in another language. This course expands the student’s intermediate communication intermediate skills in spoken Japanese and builds a larger repertoire of Kanji. Topics from Japanese 2 are reviewed with more in-depth vocabulary and structures. New topics in language and culture include target language survival level skills.

Students learn that the study of a world language not only serves as a vehicle to explore foreign cultures and ways of thinking, but also as a frame of reference for better understanding English and American “cultures” by comparison. This course is designed for students to review and reinforce previously learned structures of Japanese and acquire additional ones for successful oral and written communication. The course includes a thorough review of the writing systems introduced in Japanese 1, 2, and 3 and introduces a significant number of new kanji with an aim toward developing fluent reading comprehension of authentic written materials.

Four student foreign exchange programs are sponsored by the World Language Department with interdepartmental support from throughout the school. Students spend approximately 21⁄2 weeks living with families, attending our partner schools, and participating in activities planned by our hosts. Students participating in the French or Spanish programs must be enrolled at least in French 3 or Spanish 3. All TIE students must have and maintain a 2.5 grade point average. They must prepare reports on some aspect of life in the U.S. to be presented abroad. Regular attendance at orientation sessions and in classes at the foreign school is also required. Adherence to all TIE and SBHS program policies and the SBHS student handbook is required. Interested students submit an application form to a TIE selection committee in the spring preceding the school year in which students travel abroad.

courses.description: This course is designed to prepare students for work based learning experiences and potential internship placements. Students will engage in assessments, inventories, and activities designed to promote self-reflection and insight. Students will explore various career fields through informational interviewing and job shadowing. A variety of guest speakers will share their educational and career paths and field trips to local businesses and organizations will happen throughout the course. Additionally, students will focus on writing resumes, interviewing, professional communication, self branding, networking, and giving and getting feedback.
courses.notes: program; work-based learning

courses.description: This course holds flexible space in your schedule for you to engage in a field-based internship experience. Students will be assisted in finding placements starting with informational interviews and shadow days. Student’s readiness for an internship is determined by the level of engagement in this course and their demonstration of work readiness skills: ability to follow through, positive work ethic, integrity, self representation, and teamwork. An Internship Agreement will be completed for logistics and learning goals once an appropriate site is found. Community mentors will provide mid-point and final feedback for students.
courses.prerequisites: Students are strongly encouraged to have successfully completed the Internship: Professional Skills course prior to taking this course.
courses.notes: program; work-based learning; Students are strongly encouraged to have successfully completed the Internship: Professional Skills course prior to taking this

courses.description: Community Leadership Project is a way to bring your high school experience to a special conclusion and a chance for you to break new ground: to be curious, to take a risk, to expand your horizons, and to make a difference in your community. You will determine what your project will be, and do the critical research (community mapping, interviews, etc) needed to establish how the project will serve the greater good. From there, you will plan and execute the project with a community partner, keeping in mind that the most meaningful and helpful interventions are based in serving the needs of the identified group. Some examples of past projects include: working with a city council to combat implicit bias in the housing market; establishing an empowerment group for girls at an elementary school; being a founding member of a committee working with local and state government officials to impact educational decisions.. What will your legacy be?
